# The `inlabru` workflow

## The syntax {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"}

::: {style="height: 50px;"}
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "1,2,3"

# Define model components
comps <- component_1(...) +
  component_2(...) + 
  ...

# Define the model predictor
pred <- linear_function(component_1,
                            component_2, ...)

# Build the observation model
lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred,
               family = ... ,
               data = ... ,
                ...)

# Fit the model
fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Components**

```{r}
#| eval: false
~ my_component_name(
  main = ...,
  model = ...
)
```

- `my_component_name` how you label your component (.e.g, `beta_0`,`myspde`)
- `main` input data for the component (e.g., a the name of a column in your data or a spatial object)
- `model` The type of model component (e.g., `linear`,`fixed`,`iid`,`rw1`,`rw2`,`ar1`, see `?INLA::inla.list.models()$latent`)
:::
:::::

## The syntax {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"}

::: {style="height: 50px;"}
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "5,6,7"
#| 
# Define model components
comps <- component_1(...) +
  component_2(...) + 
  ...

# Define the model predictor
pred <- linear_function(component_1,
                            component_2, ...)

# Build the observation model
lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred,
               family = ... ,
               data = ... ,
                ...)

# Fit the model
fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**linear predictor**

- can be defined within the formula:

```{r}
#| eval: false
lik = bru_obs(formula = 
                response ~  component_1(...) + 
                component_2(...),
              family,
              data)
```

- or use a full stop short-code after the components have been defined

```{r}
#| eval: false

lik = bru_obs(formula = response ~.,
              family,
              data)
```
:::
:::::

## The syntax {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"}

::: {style="height: 50px;"}
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "9,10,11,12,13|16,17"
#| 
# Define model components
comps <- component_1(...) +
  component_2(...) + 
  ...

# Define the model predictor
pred <- linear_function(component_1,
                            component_2, ...)

# Build the observation model
lik <- bru_obs(formula = pred,
               family = ... ,
               data = ... ,
                ...)

# Fit the model
fit <- bru(comps, lik, ...)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Likelihood**

Specify the distribution family (see `inla.list.models("likelihood")`)

```{r}
#| eval: false
lik = bru_obs(formula,
              family  = "gaussian",
              data = df)
```
:::
:::::

## Why do we need the -1 in the formula? {.smaller}

- `inlabru` provides a dedicated term, `Intercept()`, for specifying an intercept that is shared across all data.

- When this term is omitted, a common intercept is added by default, unless the formula or component explicitly includes `-1`.

```{r}
df = data.frame(covariate = runif(100))
df  = df %>% mutate(y = 1 + 0.5 *covariate + rnorm(100))
```

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="33.33%"}
**Wrong** :x:

```{r}
#| echo: true
cmp = ~ beta0(1) + 
  beta1(covariate, 
  model = "linear") 

lik = bru_obs(formula = y ~ . , 
              data = df)

m1 = bru(cmp, lik)

round(m1$summary.fixed[,c(1,2)],3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="33.33%"}
**Correct** :white_check_mark:

```{r}
cmp = ~ Intercept(1) + 
  beta1(covariate,
  model = "linear")

lik = bru_obs(y~ ., 
              data = df)

m1 = bru(cmp, lik)

round(m1$summary.fixed[,c(1,2)],3)

```
:::

::: {.column width="33.33%"}
**Correct** :white_check_mark:

```{r}
cmp = ~  -1 + beta0(1) + 
  beta1(covariate, 
  model = "linear")

lik = bru_obs(y~. ,
            data = df)

m1 = bru(cmp, lik)
round(m1$summary.fixed[,c(1,2)],3)

```
:::
::::::



# Categorical variables and interactions

## Categorical variables and Interactions

`inlabru` has a specific component type for this that is called `fixed`.



Let's look at the `iris` dataset that is in `R`

```{r}

head(iris)

```




![](figures/setosa.jpg){fig-align="center"}



## Effects of categorical variables in `inlabru` {.smaller}

We want to fit a model where `Species` is the only covariate.

- `Species` has three categories: `setosa`, `versicolor` and `virginica`
- We want to model it as a factor effect

$$\begin{aligned}
y_i & \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma_y), \\
\mu_i &= \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{0,\text{versicolor}}\, x_{i2} + \beta_{0,\text{virginica}}\, x_{i3}
\end{aligned}$$
$x_{ij} = 1$ if flower $i$ belongs to species $j$ (1 = Setosa, 2 = Versicolor, 3 = Virginica) and 0 otherwise.

```{r}
#| echo: true

iris$Species = factor(iris$Species)
m1 = lm(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris)
m1$coef
```

Here *I. setosa* is our reference category!

::: fragment
How do we do this in `inlabru`?
:::

## Effects of categorical variables in `inlabru`{.smaller}

**Parametrization 1**: Reference category. Use the `fixed` model

```{r}
#| echo: true
cmp1 = ~ -1 + spp(~ Species, model = "fixed")

lik1 = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~.,
               data = iris)

fit1 = bru(cmp1, lik1)

fit1$summary.random$spp[,c(1:3)]
```

. . .

::: callout-note
- `spp(~ Species, model = "fixed")` is a `lm` style model definition! So an intercept is automatically included
- The results are stored in the `summary.random` part of the model, not the `summary.fixed`
:::

## Effects of categorical variables in `inlabru`{.smaller}

**Parametrization 2**: No reference category

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1"
cmp2 = ~ -1 + spp(~ -1 + Species, model = "fixed")

lik2 = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~.,
               data = iris)

fit2 = bru(cmp2, lik2)

fit2$summary.random$spp[,c(1:3)]
```

. . .

This is just a re-parametrization from our previous model

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

coef = fit1$summary.random$spp
c( coef[1,2],
   coef[1,2] +  coef[2,2],
   coef[1,2] +  coef[3,2])
```
:::

:::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
- $\beta_0$: mean sepal length for *I. setosa*

- $\beta_0 + \beta_{0,\text{versicolor}}$ : mean sepal length for for *I. versicolor*

- $\beta_0 + \beta_{0,\text{virginica}}$: mean sepal length for for *I. virginica*
:::
::::
::::::

## Interactions of linear covariates in `inlabru`{.smaller}

Here the easiest option is to use again the `fixed` model type.

. . .

Say we want to fit a model with interactions between (**categorical**) `Species` and and (**continuous**) `Petal.Length`.

::: panel-tabset
## `lm`

```{r}
#| echo: true
m2 = lm(Sepal.Length ~ Species * Petal.Length, data = iris)
m2$coefficients
```

## `inlabru`

```{r}
#| echo: true

cmp = ~ -1 + fixed_effects( ~ ( Species * Petal.Length), model = "fixed")
lik = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~ .,
              data = iris)
fit = bru(cmp, lik)
fit$summary.random$fixed_effects$mean
fit$summary.random$fixed_effects$sd

```
:::

# Getting results from the fitted model

## The `result` object {.smaller}

The fitted model is stored in an `inlabru` object

Let's

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

# ask inlabru to compute DIC adn WAIC
bru_options_set(control.compute = list(dic = T, waic = T))

cmp = ~ -1 + 
  spp( ~ Species, model = "fixed") +
  petal_length(Petal.Length, model = "linear") +
  petal_width(Petal.Width, model = "linear")


lik = bru_obs(formula =  Sepal.Length ~ .,
              data = iris )


result = bru(cmp, lik)
summary(result)

```

## Getting results I {.smaller}

Some results are very easy to get as they are contained in the `result` object:

- Summaries for fixed effects

```{r}
#| echo: true
result$summary.fixed
```

. . .

- Summaries for random effects

```{r}
#| echo: true
result$summary.random$spp
```

. . .

- Summaries for hyperparameters

```{r}
#| echo: true
result$summary.hyperpar
```

## Getting results I {.smaller}

- Marginals for fixed effects

```{r}
#| echo: true
result$marginals.fixed$petal_width[1:3,]
result$marginals.fixed$petal_length[1:3,]

```

. . .

- Summaries for random effects

```{r}
#| echo: true
result$marginals.random$spp$index.1[1:3,]
```

. . .

- Summaries for hyperparameters

```{r}
#| echo: true
result$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for the Gaussian observations`[1:3,]
```

## `predict()` and `generate()` functions {.smaller}

Often one wants more "complex" results from the model.

Suppose we fit a model with the following linear predictor

$$\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Species}_i} +  \beta_{1,\text{Species}_i}\text{Petal Length}_i,\ i =1,\dots,n$$

We might want to recover the three regression lines

- $\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Setosa}} +  \beta_{1,\text{Setosa}}\text{Petal Length}_i$
- $\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Virginica}} +  \beta_{1,\text{Virginica}}\text{Petal Length}_i$
- $\eta_i = \beta_{0,\text{Versicolor}} +  \beta_{1,\text{Versicolor}}\text{Petal Length}_i$

. . .

To do this we can use the `predict()` and `generate()` functions.

- `predict()` *simulates* from the fitted posterior distribution $\pi(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{u},\theta)$, computes what you ask and produces a summary of the samples (mean, sd, quantiles, etc)

- `generate()` *simulates* from the fitted posterior distribution $\pi(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{u},\theta)$, computes what you ask and return the samples!

## Example 1 - predictions for the mean

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true


cmp = ~ -1 + fixed_effects(~Species * Petal.Length, model = "fixed")

lik = bru_obs(formula = Sepal.Length ~ .,
              data = iris)

fit = bru(cmp, lik)

pred_grid <- iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  reframe(Petal.Length = seq(min(Petal.Length), 
                             max(Petal.Length), by = 0.1))

res = predict(fit, pred_grid, ~ fixed_effects)

res[1:5,]

```

## Example 1 - predictions for the mean

Notice that we predict only within the range of the covariate for each species:

```{r}
#| echo: true
res %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(Petal.Length, mean, group = Species, color = Species)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(Petal.Length, ymin = q0.025 , ymax = q0.975,
                  group = Species, fill = Species), alpha = 0.5)+
  facet_wrap(~Species,scales="free_x")
  
```

## Example 1 - predictions for new observations

The uncertainty we have computed now is relative to the prediction of $\eta$.

- If we want to predict a new observation, we need to add the observation (likelihood) uncertainty $\sigma^2_y$
- We compute a prediction interval using `generate()`:

```{r}

q_samples = generate(fit, pred_grid,
                    formula = ~ {
                      eta = fixed_effects
                      sigma = sqrt(1/Precision_for_the_Gaussian_observations)
                      c(qnorm(0.025, eta, sigma), qnorm(0.975, eta, sigma))
                      },
         n.samples = 1000)


pred_int = cbind(pred_grid,
                 matrix(rowMeans(q_samples), ncol = 2,
                        dimnames = list(NULL, c("lower", "upper"))))

```



## Example 1 - predictions for new observations

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length,color = Species)) +
  geom_line(data=res, aes(Petal.Length, mean, group = Species, color = Species))+
  geom_ribbon(data=res,aes(Petal.Length, ymin = q0.025 , ymax = q0.975,
                  group = Species, fill = Species), alpha = 0.5)+
  geom_line(data = pred_int,aes(Petal.Length, lower),
               color = "red",lty=2) + 
   geom_line(data = pred_int,aes(Petal.Length, upper),
               color = "red",lty=2) + 
  facet_wrap(~Species,scales="free_x")
```

## Example 2 {.smaller}

We will look at the effect that incubation temperature has on the sex determination of turtles. Lets say we are interested in the number male turtles out of the total number of turtles that hatched.

```{r}
data(turtle, package = "faraway")

turtle$total  <- turtle$male + turtle$female
turtle$temp_c <- turtle$temp - mean(turtle$temp)
glimpse(turtle)

```

![](figures/turtles.jpg){fig-align="center"}

## Example 2 {.smaller}

We begin fitting a logistic regression of the form:

$$\begin{aligned}
y_i \mid \eta_i &\sim \text{Binomial}(n_i, p_i)\\
\eta_i  &= \text{logit}(p_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{temperature}_i
\end{aligned}$$

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: ""
cmp = ~ -1 + beta_0(1) + beta_1(temp, model = "linear")

lik = bru_obs(formula = male ~ beta_0 + beta_1,
              data = turtle,
              family = "binomial",
              Ntrials = turtle$total)
fit_turtles = bru(cmp, lik)

```

We now want to extract results...what do we want?

. . .

- The temperature effect $\beta_1 \text{temperature}_i$ ?
- The linear predictor $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{temperature}_i$?
- The estimated probability off a male being hatched $p_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)$ ?

We can get all of them with the `predict()` or `generate()` functions!

## Example - `predict()`

```{r}
turtle_pred <- data.frame(temp = seq(27,30,0.1))

preds1 = predict(object = fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ beta_1)
preds2 = predict(object = fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ beta_0 + beta_1)
inv_logit = function(x) ((1 + exp(-x))^(-1))
preds3 = predict(object = fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred, ~ inv_logit(beta_0 + beta_1))

```

or

```{r}
preds = predict( fit_turtles, newdata = turtle_pred,
                ~ data.frame(temp_eff = beta_1,
                             lin_pred = beta_0 + beta_1,
                             probs = inv_logit(beta_0 + beta_1)),
                n.samples = 1000
                )

round(preds$probs[1:3,],3)
```

## Example - `predict()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
preds$probs %>% ggplot() + geom_line(aes(temp, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(temp, ymin = q0.025, ymax = q0.975), alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(y="p",x= "Temperature")

```

## Example - `generate()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

samples = generate(fit_turtles, newdata =  turtle_pred, ~ 
                  data.frame(temp_eff = beta_1,
                             lin_pred = beta_0 + beta_1,
                             probs = inv_logit(beta_0 + beta_1)),
               n.samples = 20)


# samples is now a list of length 20 (n.samples) each element of the list looks like:

samples[[1]][1:3,]
```

## Example - `generate()`

```{r}
#| echo: true

data.frame(temp = turtle_pred$temp, sapply(samples, function(x) x$probs)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-temp) %>%
  ggplot() + geom_line(aes(temp, value, group = name, color = factor(name))) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

# Manipulating posterior marginals

## Manipulating posterior marginals

We can be interested in functions of the posterior marginals that are computed by the `bru()` function.

For example, we might want to :

- compute the mean of a posterior marginal
- compute the median of a posterior marginal
- sample from the posterior marginal
- ...

All this can be done with the help of the `inla.*marginal()` family of functions

## Example from the iris data {auto-animate=TRUE}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}

<br>



::: {style="font-size:0.7em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1"
post_prec = fit$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for the Gaussian observations`  # <1>

post_sd = inla.tmarginal(fun = function(x) 1/sqrt(x), post_prec) 

post_sd_mode = inla.mmarginal(post_sd)

post_sd_mean = inla.emarginal(fun =function(x)x, post_sd )

post_sd_sample = inla.rmarginal(1000, post_sd)


```

<br>

1.  Obtain the posterior marginal for the *standard deviation* of the observation error $\sigma^2_y$
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.7em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| 
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = post_prec,aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  labs(x= expression(1/sigma^2))
  
```
:::
::::
:::::::





## Example from the iris data {auto-animate=TRUE}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
post_prec = fit$marginals.hyperpar$`Precision for the Gaussian observations`  # <1>

post_sd = inla.tmarginal(fun = function(x) 1/sqrt(x), post_prec) #<2>

post_sd_mode = inla.mmarginal(post_sd)

post_sd_mean = inla.emarginal(fun =function(x)x, post_sd )

post_sd_sample = inla.rmarginal(1000, post_sd)


```

<br>

1.  Obtain the posterior marginal for the *standard deviation* of the observation error $\sigma^2_y$
2.  Transform back to SD scale

:::
::::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.7em;"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = post_sd,aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  labs(x= expression(sigma))


```
:::
::::
:::::::

```{r}
ggplot() +
   geom_histogram(data = 
            data.frame(samples = post_sd_sample),
                 aes(x = samples,
                     y = after_stat(density)),
                 fill = "lightblue" ,alpha=0.75)+
  geom_line(data = post_sd,aes(x=x,y=y)) +
  labs(x= expression(sigma))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = post_sd_mode,
             color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = post_sd_mean,
             color = "blue") 
 


```
:::
::::
:::::::




## The `inla.*marginal()` family

<br>


::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}
| **Function Name** | **Usage** |
|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| `inla.dmarginal(x, marginal, ...)` | Density at a vector of evaluation points $x$ |
| `inla.pmarginal(q, marginal, ...)` | Distribution function at a vector of quantiles *q* |
| `inla.qmarginal(p, marginal, ...)` | Quantile function at a vector of probabilities *p* |
| `inla.rmarginal(n, marginal)` | Generate *n* random deviates |
| `inla.hpdmarginal(p, marginal, ...)` | Compute the highest posterior density interval at level *p* |
| `inla.emarginal(fun, marginal, ...)` | Compute the expected value assuming transformation given by *fun* |
| `inla.mmarginal(marginal)` | Computes the mode |
| `inla.smarginal(marginal, ...)` | Smoothed density (returns x-values and interpolated y-values) |
| `inla.tmarginal(fun, marginal, ...)` | Transform the marginal using function *fun* |
| `inla.zmarginal(marginal)` | Summary statistics for the marginal |
:::

# Getting help while using `inlabru`

## Which priors have I used?

<br>

You might wonder which priors have you used in your model..

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit = bru(cmp, lik)

INLA::inla.priors.used(fit)

```

**NB** `inla.priors.used` is a function of the `INLA` package, so you need to load it explicitly.

:::{.fragment}
In the following practical we will see how to change the default priors in INLA.
:::


## Getting help!


<br>
<br>

The `inla.doc()` function provides help on the different prior, latent models and likelihood.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

inla.doc("ar1")
inla.doc("pc.prior")
inla.doc("gaussian")
```

## Which models are implemented?

**Likelihoods**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
# which likelihoods?
inla.list.models("likelihood")
```

## Which models are implemented?

**Components**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
# which latent models? (components)
inla.list.models("latent")
```

## Which models are implemented?

**Priors**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
# which priors?
inla.list.models("prior")
```

# Take home message

## Take home message


<br>

- Linear models with interactions

  - `inlabru` has a special model to implement this

- `predict()` and `generate()` functions are powerful tools (based on sampling from the posterior distribution) to obtain many interesting results!

-  There a multiple was to manipulate directly the posterior marginal distribution of our parameters.
